title: Scaling and load balancing
text: Vertical scaling adds CPU or memory to one machine and hits a hardware ceiling. Horizontal scaling adds more machines and requires stateless services so any server can handle any request. A load balancer distributes traffic using algorithms such as round robin or least connections and removes servers that fail health checks, which also gives availability.

title: Caching, CAP theorem and URL shortener design
text: A cache such as Redis stores hot results in fast memory. Entries expire by TTL or are invalidated on writes, at the risk of stale data. The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a distributed system must choose consistency or availability. A URL shortener generates unique base62 ids, stores id to URL in a key-value store, caches popular links and uses replicas or a CDN because reads dominate.

title: Authentication, authorization and password storage
text: Authentication proves who a user is and authorization decides what they may do. Never store passwords in plain text. Hash them with a slow, salted algorithm such as bcrypt or argon2 with a unique salt per password and compare hashes at login. To resist brute force and credential stuffing, rate limit by account and IP, add delays or lockouts, require multi-factor authentication and block known breached passwords.

title: Injection, CORS and CSRF
text: Injection happens when untrusted input changes the meaning of a query. Use parameterized queries, validate input, run the database with least privilege and, for MongoDB, reject operator objects such as $ne in user input. CORS is a browser policy that controls which origins can read responses. CSRF tricks a browser into sending an authenticated request with its cookies, and is prevented with SameSite cookies or CSRF tokens. CORS does not stop CSRF.

title: Unit, integration and API testing
text: Unit tests check one function in isolation and are fast. Integration tests check several parts together and find wiring problems. Mocks and stubs replace external dependencies such as payments or email so tests stay fast and deterministic, and contract tests keep mocks accurate. Test Express endpoints with Supertest against a separate test database, asserting status and body for success, auth failure and invalid input.

title: Test pyramid and flaky tests
text: The test pyramid recommends many unit tests, fewer integration tests and few end-to-end tests, because higher levels are slower and more brittle. Flaky tests are caused by timing, shared state, real network calls and randomness. Fix them by isolating state, controlling the clock and avoiding real external calls. A CI pipeline runs lint and tests on every pull request before deploying.

title: Docker and configuration
text: Docker packages an app with its dependencies into a container that behaves the same on every machine. An image is a read-only template built in layers from a Dockerfile, and a container is a running instance. Order Dockerfile steps so cached layers are reused. Keep configuration in environment variables, never commit secrets, use a secret manager in production and rotate secrets.

title: Zero-downtime deployment and incident response
text: Zero-downtime deployment uses rolling or blue-green releases, health checks before traffic shifts, backward-compatible database migrations and a quick rollback plan. When latency spikes, check dashboards and metrics, compare with recent deploys and config changes, inspect logs and traces, and look at saturated resources or slow dependencies such as the database. Mitigate or roll back first, then find the root cause.

title: Variables, closures and this
text: var is function scoped and hoisted as undefined, while let and const are block scoped and const cannot be reassigned. A closure is a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope ended, and enables private state. The value of this depends on how a function is called; call, apply and bind set it explicitly and arrow functions use the surrounding this. Objects inherit through the prototype chain.

title: Promises and the event loop
text: A promise represents a future value that is pending, fulfilled or rejected. async and await is syntax over promises, errors are handled with try and catch, and Promise.all runs independent tasks in parallel. JavaScript has one thread and an event loop. After each macrotask such as a timer or event, all microtasks, which are promise callbacks, run before the next macrotask.

title: Virtual DOM, props, state and effects
text: React keeps a virtual DOM, compares the new tree with the previous one and updates only the changed parts of the real DOM. Props are read-only inputs and state is owned by the component; update state through its setter, never by mutation. useEffect runs side effects after render, re-runs when values in its dependency array change, and its cleanup function removes subscriptions or timers. Missing dependencies cause stale values.

title: Re-rendering and large app structure
text: A component re-renders when its state, props, context or parent changes. React.memo skips renders when props are shallow equal, useMemo caches expensive values and useCallback keeps function references stable, but they help only when measured. For large apps organize code by feature, split routes with lazy and Suspense, keep server state separate from UI state, use error boundaries and write tests.

title: Box model, flexbox, grid and responsive design
text: Every element is a box with content, padding, border and margin, and box-sizing border-box includes padding and border in the width. Flexbox is one-dimensional and suits components, while grid is two-dimensional and suits page layouts. Specificity ranks inline styles above ids, ids above classes and classes above elements. Build responsive pages mobile-first with relative units, flexible layouts and media queries.

title: Accessibility
text: Use semantic HTML first. Custom widgets such as dropdowns need full keyboard support with Tab, arrow keys, Enter and Escape, ARIA attributes such as aria-expanded to expose state, visible focus management and sufficient color contrast. Test with a screen reader and keyboard only.

title: Loading performance and Core Web Vitals
text: Page speed depends on asset size, number of requests, server response time and render-blocking resources. Use compression, caching and optimized images. Code splitting with dynamic import and lazy loading defers work until needed and shrinks the initial bundle. Core Web Vitals are LCP for loading of main content, INP for responsiveness and CLS for layout stability.

title: Debounce, throttle and large lists
text: Debounce waits until activity stops before running, which suits search inputs. Throttle runs at most once per interval, which suits scroll and resize handlers. For a long list, profile first, then virtualize so only visible rows render, paginate or load incrementally, memoize row components with stable keys and avoid needless parent re-renders.

title: Lifting state, context and Redux
text: Lifting state up means moving shared state to the nearest common parent. Context avoids prop drilling for rarely changing values such as theme or the logged-in user, but all consumers re-render when the value changes. In Redux, components dispatch actions, pure reducers compute the next state from the previous state and the action, and the store notifies subscribers. Reducers must never mutate state.

title: Server state and optimistic updates
text: Server state is remote data that can become stale, unlike local UI state. Libraries like React Query provide caching, request deduplication, background refetching, invalidation and loading and error states. An optimistic update changes the UI immediately, keeps a snapshot, rolls back and shows an error if the request fails, and reconciles with the server response.

title: TypeScript types and generics
text: TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript, catches errors at compile time and improves editor tooling. Interfaces and type aliases both describe shapes; interfaces can be extended and merged while type aliases can also name unions and primitives. Generics make code reusable while preserving type information, for example identity<T>(x: T): T, and can be constrained with extends.

title: Narrowing and API contracts
text: any disables type checking, unknown forces narrowing before use and never marks impossible values. Narrow types with typeof, instanceof and discriminated unions. Keep frontend and backend consistent by defining the API contract once, for example in a schema or OpenAPI file, deriving types from it, using Pick, Omit and Partial for variants and validating at runtime at the boundary, for instance with zod.

title: XSS, token storage and CSP
text: Cross-site scripting lets an attacker run script in other users' browsers through unescaped content, so escape and sanitize output. Tokens in localStorage can be read by any script and are exposed to XSS, while httpOnly cookies cannot be read by JavaScript but should be Secure and SameSite to limit CSRF. A Content Security Policy header restricts where scripts and resources may load from, blocks inline scripts and limits XSS damage.

title: OAuth for SPAs and dependency risk
text: A single-page app should use the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE, not the implicit flow, with short-lived access tokens, validated state and redirect URIs, refresh tokens in httpOnly cookies or behind a backend-for-frontend, and proper logout and revocation. To reduce npm supply chain risk, respect the lockfile, audit dependencies, keep few well-maintained packages and review updates.

title: Learning types and overfitting
text: Supervised learning uses labeled data, unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards by interacting with an environment. Overfitting means the model performs well on training data but poorly on new data, while underfitting performs poorly on both. Compare training and validation error; fix overfitting with more data, regularization or a simpler model and underfitting with more capacity or better features.

title: Bias-variance, regularization and dimensionality
text: Bias is error from overly simple assumptions and variance is sensitivity to the training set; simple models have high bias and complex models high variance. L1 regularization penalizes absolute weights and gives sparse models, while L2 penalizes squared weights and shrinks them smoothly. In high dimensions data becomes sparse and distances lose meaning, so more data is needed; PCA projects data onto directions of maximum variance.

title: Classification metrics
text: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct, recall is the share of actual positives found, and F1 is their harmonic mean. With imbalanced classes accuracy is misleading because predicting the majority class scores well. The ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate across thresholds and AUC summarizes ranking quality. For rare positives the precision-recall curve is more informative.

title: Validation, leakage and thresholds
text: Split data into training, validation and test sets; the test set gives the final unbiased estimate and must not be used for tuning. K-fold cross-validation rotates validation folds for a stable estimate. Data leakage occurs when outside information influences training, for example scaling before splitting, so fit preprocessing inside each fold. Choose the decision threshold from the cost of false positives and false negatives, calibrate probabilities and keep monitoring.

title: Linear and logistic regression
text: Linear regression fits a linear relationship to a continuous target by minimizing mean squared error and is sensitive to outliers. Logistic regression passes a linear combination of features through a sigmoid to output a probability, uses a threshold to choose a class and is trained with log loss.

title: Trees, ensembles and SVM
text: A decision tree splits data on the feature that best separates the classes but overfits easily. A random forest averages many trees trained on random samples and features, reducing variance. Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially, each correcting the previous errors, and needs tuning of learning rate and depth. An SVM finds the maximum-margin hyperplane defined by support vectors; the kernel trick lets it separate non-linear data using kernels such as RBF.

title: Neural networks and gradient descent
text: A neural network is layers of weighted neurons, and activation functions such as ReLU add non-linearity; without them the network is a linear model. Gradient descent updates weights against the loss gradient; the learning rate sets the step size, with too large diverging and too small training slowly. Mini-batch SGD and Adam are common optimizers. Backpropagation applies the chain rule backward from the loss to get every gradient.

title: CNNs and gradient problems
text: Convolutional networks slide small shared filters over images, detecting local patterns with few parameters and some translation invariance, and pooling reduces spatial size. In deep networks gradients can vanish or explode. Mitigate with ReLU activations, careful initialization, batch or layer normalization, residual connections, gradient clipping, and LSTM or GRU units for sequences.

title: Text representation and embeddings
text: Tokenization splits text into tokens. Bag-of-words counts words ignoring order, and TF-IDF weights words by frequency in a document and rarity across documents. Word embeddings such as Word2Vec and GloVe are dense vectors where similar words are close together, unlike sparse one-hot vectors that carry no similarity.

title: Transformers, attention and RAG
text: RNNs and LSTMs process tokens sequentially, cannot be parallelized and struggle with long-range dependencies. Transformers use self-attention: each token produces query, key and value vectors, attention weights come from query-key similarity and the output is a weighted sum of values; multiple heads learn different relations and positional encoding supplies order. Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant chunks and adds them to the prompt to reduce hallucination; evaluate retrieval with recall@k and answers for faithfulness and relevance.

title: Pipelines, versioning and serving
text: An ML pipeline covers data collection and cleaning, feature engineering, training and validation, deployment and monitoring. Version code with git, data with a tool such as DVC and models and metrics with an experiment tracker such as MLflow, and record hyperparameters and seeds for reproducibility. Batch serving scores records on a schedule and is simpler; real-time serving answers each request through an API and needs low latency.

title: Drift, monitoring and retraining
text: Data drift is a change in the input distribution and concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and the target. Monitor feature distributions with statistical tests, track prediction quality as labels arrive and alert or retrain when thresholds are crossed. A release pipeline validates data, trains automatically, compares the candidate with the current model, promotes via a model registry with shadow or A/B rollout and rolls back automatically if quality drops.
